title: Maximizers and Satisficers
text:
The economist and psychologist Herbert Simon had argued in the 1950s that people often "satisfice": instead of searching for the best possible option, they settle on one that is good enough. In 2002 Barry Schwartz of Swarthmore College and colleagues, including Sonja Lyubomirsky and Darrin Lehman, asked what happens to people who do the opposite.

They built a questionnaire to measure the tendency to maximize, with statements such as "When I watch TV, I channel surf, often scanning through the available options even while attempting to watch one program" and "I never settle for second best." Well over a thousand people in the United States and Canada filled it out, along with measures of happiness, optimism, depression and regret.

People who scored high as maximizers reported less happiness, less optimism and less satisfaction with life, and more depression and regret, than satisficers. In follow-up studies, maximizers compared themselves with others more often and were more sensitive to how others were doing. In shopping, they considered more options and were more likely to imagine alternatives they had not chosen, which made them less pleased with what they bought.

Schwartz argued that in a world of abundant choice, holding out for the best can be a recipe for misery. A study he later coauthored on graduating students found that maximizers landed jobs with higher starting salaries but felt worse about the outcome than satisficers did.
lesson: For most choices, decide what good enough looks like before you start searching, take the first option that meets it, and stop comparing. Save maximizing for the few decisions that truly matter.
people: Barry Schwartz, Andrew Ward, John Monterosso, Sonja Lyubomirsky, Katherine White, Darrin Lehman
location: Swarthmore College, Pennsylvania, USA, and Canada
source: Schwartz, B., Ward, A., Monterosso, J., Lyubomirsky, S., White, K., and Lehman, D. R. (2002). Maximizing versus satisficing: Happiness is a matter of choice. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 83(5), 1178-1197.
caveat: The findings are correlational, and later work found the maximizing scale mixes high standards (fairly harmless) with exhaustive searching and decision difficulty (more harmful).
